content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper seeks to solve calibration on out-of-distribution data by a proposed method called adaptive calibrator ensemble (ACE). It trains 2 models: one for in-distribution data and one or modified in-distribution data where the correctly classified samples have been downweighted. The average predicted confidence on the test data compared to the training data is then used as a way to find the right balance for weighted averaging of these 2 models. The method is compared against Perturbation and TransCal as existing methods, on top of multiple standard post-hoc calibration methods, demonstrating improved performance as measured by ECE.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The proposed method is simple and intuitive.
2. The relevant literature has been covered sufficiently except for the paper by Gong et al from ICCV2021 [1].
3. The experiments have been performed with several datasets and there are comparisons against existing methods, except with methods from [1].

Weaknesses:
* The paper concentrates on ECE but does not report accuracy at the same time. Is accuracy different for different methods, such as Spline, Spline+ACE, Spline+Perturbation? It is important not to sacrifice too much accuracy when improving calibration.

* The most important weakness is that the paper fails to compare against the state-of-the-art methods proposed by [1] Gong et al from ICCV2021 which in that paper improved significantly over TransCal. The methods in [1] can work even 1 test instance at a time, not requiring a batch or the full test set.

* The experimental setup has not been justified well enough. Why have the methods Ensemble, SVI, SVI-AvUTS, SVI-AvUC been left out from the comparisons in Table 2, whereas they are present in Table 3? Why has the method Spline+Perturbation not been included in Table 3 whereas it is present in Table 2?

* Based on Figure 3b, the method of Eq.(6) (not Eq.(5) as stated in the caption of the figure) used for choosing the value of $\alpha$ is so far from optimal that even choosing a constant value of $alpha=0.3$ would probably have given better results on average across all datasets. Same kind of curves would be good to see for other architectures and datasets though, e.g. in the appendix. However, I cannot recommend a better way of choosing $\alpha$, so I cannot criticize too much either. Still, if the choice of $\alpha$ is quite arbitrary then the justification for the whole method is undermined.

* The authors claim that $d=10$ resulting in 9.09% accuracy is effective without being specific about what dataset this is about. It seems problematic for datasets like CIFAR-10 with only 10 classes, because this accuracy would already be worse than random.

Minor weaknesses:

* The paragraph starting with "Plain fact: individual samples matter in the classification loss" feels very strange to me. First, this very statement that individual samples matter is obviously true for NLL, because the loss is 0 only if the model predicts correctly with full confidence equal to 1, which almost never occurs in practice. The claims "If a sample is correctly classified, the classification loss will likely return a small value; If a sample is incorrectly classified, there will likely be a high loss value" are also so obviously true that it is strange that these have been even stated, thus potentially creating confusion. It would at least be better if the authors would have mentioned that NLL is a monotonic function of the probability predicted for the actual class, and thus it is obvious that if the probability is above 50% (low NLL) then the prediction must be correct, or if it is below $1/n$ where $n$ is the number of classes (i.e. high NLL), then the prediction must be wrong, and between 50% and $1/n$ it could be correct or wrong, tending to be more correct for higher probabilities and more wrong for lower probabilities. Then it would at least be clearer for the reader. Because currently it sounds like a discovery that can only be made after performing an experiment and looking at its results in Figure 1a.

* It is a bit odd to read "By adjusting $N_F/N_T$" before it has been explained what is going on, because typically $N_F$ and $N_T$ are quantities that are not directly under the control of the user.

* "the difficulty of a dataset (with respect to a classifier) shares the same meaning as classifier accuracy on this dataset" is a confusing claim after defining difficulty as $N_F/N_T$. A more precise statement would be that these concepts are in a one-to-one mapping.

* "calibration accuracy" can be a confusing term

* Red/green triangles are used in a counterintuitive way in Table 1. I would have used them exactly oppositely, i.e. a green downwards arrow means that the performance is improved since the loss has gone down.

[1] Gong, Y.; Lin, X.; Yao, Y.; Dietterich, T. G.; Divakaran, A.; and Gervasio, M. 2021. Confidence Calibration for Domain Generalization under Covariate Shift. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision, 8958–8967.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Except for the weaknesses above, the paper is sufficiently clearly written. The paper is novel and reproducible, but there are some issues with quality as stated above.
content.summary_of_the_review: It is not clear whether the proposed methods are better than those proposed by Gong et al [1] (see the reference above) which I suspect is a paper that the authors have simply not been aware of. This is unfortunate, because that method improved significantly over TransCal which the current paper also compares against. Furthermore, Gong et al [1] only needs a single test instance at a time, not a batch like the current paper. There are also some additional shortcomings in the experimental setup as discussed above.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the difficulty level of addressing the OOD problem in calibrations. The difficulty level is attractive for its simple calculation and usage in an unsupervised manner. It requires only the data instance to be applied. Previous works have limitations since they did not address the various range of OOD or require additional learning on OOD data sets. The proposed algorithm ACE consists of a combination of two calibrators trained on an easy data set and the most difficulty dataset. The mixing ratio is determined by the (roughly speaking) confidence of prediction on OOD. Intensive experiments including large datasets and baseline algorithms were conducted. In addition, the effect of hyperparameters was studied. All results show the superiority of the proposed algorithm, and some datasets can not be improved by a large margin because the proposed algorithm cannot cover all OOD.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
The idea is very simple, and extensive experiments can show promising results. The numerical studies show that the ACE can be robust to in-distribution and out-of-distribution. 

Cons:
In the aspect of algorithm, the linear combination of two calibrators can be reasonable, and other types are explored in Appendix. However, the combination of two calibrators can be done in various ways. It can be done in log scale or exponential scale and others. When the combinations can have different scales, what happens? Is there another way to make the difficulty set? In my opinion, it is not completely explored or examined to make a more optimal algorithm.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: 
There is no vague paragraph or non-parsing expression. All are clarified except for the explanation in figure 3 (b). The authors said that computed $\alpha$ by the algorithm is near optimal. However, I cannot find that the optimum in dense samples is near computed $\alpha$. For example, in imageNet-R, two alpha seems very different. Please explain the graph in a more detailed manner. 
 
Quality:
Well-written. The organization of the papers seems good, and Section 3.5 Discussion can be strengthened.

Novelty and reproducibility:
The algorithm itself can be considered as the use of measuring the different distributions using the classifiers. The main novelty is the use of this measure for OOD calibration. It seems that there is no severe problem in reproducibility
content.summary_of_the_review: I prefer a simple and practical algorithm. In my opinion, this paper has great potential, shown in the experiments. My suggestion is to investigate the various way to combine two calibrators. This paper can be strong with the supplementary studies in this area.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed an post-hoc calibration method called adaptive calibration ensemble (ACE), which is shown to perform better on out-of-distribution (OOD) test sets and also doesn’t compromise performance in test sets that are in-distribution (hence adaptive). 

The basic idea is to artificially construct hard OOD calibration set in the sense that the ratio between wrong-classified examples and correct-classified examples is high (e.g., 10), and train calibrator on original calibration set and the constructed OOD set, and then return the convex combination of the two calibrator, where the coefficient is adaptively estimated with the ratio of average confidence on test set and the original calibration set.  It is intended to be a meta-algorithm that can be combined with any other post-hoc calibration methods to achieve better OOD calibration performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
* the proposed approach is simple yet demonstrated perform well empirically in certain cases
* it’s shown to improve calibration performance on OOD set w/o compromising that on in-distribution test set

Weakness
* The idea is somewhat ad-hoc and heuristic
* only tested on ImageNet, but not other datasets or even other domains, the hyperparameter d seems to be highly customized for ImageNet, it’s not clear how we should choose this parameter given any machine learning application.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
clarity: the paper is well written with clear notations and flow of logic
quality: it’s more of a empirical study on a limited domain based on a heuristic approach w/o much theoretical insights
novelty: the approach is novel at best of my knowledge 
reproducibility: I believe this work is reproducible
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper presents an adaptive approach to improving calibration on OOD dataset, through the lens of calibration set difficulty. The idea is somewhat heuristic and the empirical study is somewhat limited in the sense that it’s only in one type of datasets (ImageNet) with customized settings. While the limitation of the proposed method is acknowledged and briefly discussed, it’s lacking in-depth analysis both theoretically and empirically on how we should (or should not) apply such a method in a more general setting. 

questions
* Why do we assume OOD is always higher difficulty? Is it possible that alpha > 1?
* the results only show ECE results; wonder how it affects post-cali accuracy? 
* curious to see the correlation of alpha and the improvement magnitude. Is it the case that ACE improves more on a more-OOD set and alpha is also smaller?

typos
Intro: “aims to connect” or “correct”?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper concerns the calibration problem of a binary classifier, in the context where the test data may be from a different distribution from the training data. The goal is to make the calibration robust to these out-of-distribution (OOD) test data. The main idea is to generate synthetic OOD by subsampling in-distribution data with a different proportion of correctly and incorrectly classified instances. Two calibrators based on multiple synthetic test data that represent in-distributed and extremely OOD data respectively are computed, and the final calibrator is made to be a convex combination of the two calibrators. The weight in the convex combination is set to be the ratio between the average confidence between the two test data sets. Experiments are conducted to show the robustness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+1: the paper is easy to read, even for people not familiar with calibration.
+2: the idea is very straightforward and intuitive.

-1: there is no theoretical analysis of the proposed method, only numerical experiments.
-2: there is no theoretical justification for the choice of the weight in the ensemble calibrator. Why the ratio? Why not some other functions, such as the square of the ratio? Moreover, if D_test = D_h, then intuitively the correct weight should be alpha=0. But according to definition (6) alpha will not be 0 unless the average confidence of D_h is 0.
-3: while sampling the data based on whether an instance is correctly or incorrectly classifier is one useful way of generating synthetic OOD data, there are many other different mechanisms in which OOD data can differ from the training data. For example, there are covariate shifts, posterior drift, etc. As a consequence, the proposed method is only robust with respect to varying classification difficulty, and may not be robust in the presence of other forms of OOD data. 
-4: the paper is not most relevant to the theme of ICLR, which should focus on learning representation or deep learning. Except that the paper uses a few large image datasets and use deep learning to compute the initial classifier, there is nothing about learning representation in the proposed method.
-5: notations: In (3) and (4), what do \sum_{i}^{N_T} and \sum_{i}^{N_F} mean? Do you mean \sum_{i \in N_T} and \sum_{i \in N_F}?
-6: notations: a few notations made me confused. There are first of all two calibration sets D0 which is in distribution (original) and Dh which is OOD. Then you said "D_test is a new test set that is either in-distribution or OOD" Do you mean that D_test can be either D0 or D_h or somewhere in between?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written.
The quality/novelty of the paper is limited, as the proposed method is based on a heuristic with no theoretical guarantee. Moreover, the proposed method is restricted to one particular way of generating OOD data.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposed an ensemble calibrator based on a linear combination of two calibrators computed from two extreme test data cases. The hard extreme case is generated by subsampling the original calibration data set so that the classification difficulty increases significantly. While the proposed method is illustrated by numerical studies, there is no theoretical analysis, and the proposed method is based on a pure heuristic and is only restricted to one particular type of OOD data.

content.title: On the Calibration Set Difficulty and Out-of-distribution Calibration
content.TL;DR: Calibration set difficulity impacts out-of-distribution calibration performance
content.abstract: Model calibration usually requires optimizing some parameters (e.g., temperature) w.r.t an objective function (e.g., negative log-likelihood). In this paper, we report a plain, important but often neglected fact that the objective function is influenced by calibration set difficulty, i.e., the ratio of the number of incorrectly classified samples to that of correctly classified samples. If a test set has a drastically different difficulty level from the calibration set, the optimal calibration parameters of the two datasets would be different. In other words, a calibrator optimal on the calibration set would be suboptimal on the OOD test set and thus has degraded performance. With this knowledge, we propose a simple and effective method named adaptive calibrator ensemble (ACE) to calibrate OOD datasets whose difficulty is usually higher than the calibration set. Specifically, two calibration functions are trained, one for in-distribution data (low difficulty), and the other for severely OOD data (high difficulty). To achieve desirable calibration on a new OOD dataset, ACE uses an adaptive weighting method that strikes a balance between the two extreme functions. When plugged in, ACE generally improves the performance of a few state-of-the-art calibration schemes on a series of OOD benchmarks. Importantly, such improvement does not come at the cost of the in-distribution calibration accuracy.
